extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigants, and practitioners involved in Korean patent litigation (revocation, invalidation, and infringement proceedings)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards governing revocation (administrative) suits, civil patent/infringement actions, evidence, hearings, claim construction, defenses, venue, and case management in the Republic of Korea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit may argue substantive or procedural unlawfulness in an IPTAB decision; the litigant may argue and prove reasons for unlawfulness even if the IPTAB did not rule on those reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court presiding over the revocation suit may examine and decide on such reasons and take them as the basis for its decision unless special circumstances counsel otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on raising new grounds by the defendant (KIPO Commissioner)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner of the KIPO may not raise a new ground of rejection in a revocation suit that was not raised before the examiner or the IPTAB because the plaintiff was not given an opportunity to submit opinion disputing the new ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation protects applicants' procedural rights; however, if the new grounds are in line with the essence of notified grounds and the applicant previously had opportunity to comment (i.e., are supplementary), such grounds may be admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of a revocation complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must describe in detail: procedural background on the IPTAB trial; summary of the administrative decision (arguments and IPTAB decision); parts admitted and not admitted among grounds; all arguments for revocation; notice of related cases; plaintiff's opinion on overall proceedings including any plan to request evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also attach basic evidentiary documents and requisites such as power of attorney, corporate register/certificate of nationality (for foreign parties), certificate of service of administrative decision; and specific exhibits depending on the type of revocation (rejection, invalidation, scope of rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required attachments for different revocation types
rubrics_metrics.description: For rejection revocation: IPTAB decision, patent application, examiner’s preliminary rejection, amendment, opinion and final rejection; for invalidation revocation: IPTAB decision, original register, publication of registration and evidence relating to prior art; for scope-of-rights revocation: IPTAB decision, original register, publication of registration, explanatory documents and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure none of these basic evidentiary documents or requisite attachments are overlooked when filing the complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of lodging a revocation suit on IPTAB decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a revocation suit is lodged, the IPTAB decision subject to revocation is prevented from being treated as final and conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Court requires that the purpose of a revocation suit (or appeal) be notified to the President of the IPTAB without delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's answer requirements and deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant must submit an answer no later than three weeks from service of plaintiff’s complaint or brief containing the specific cause of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer must include: response to plaintiff’s demand; parts admitted/not admitted; detailed rebuttal arguments on non-admitted parts; other arguments to maintain the decision; notice of related cases; acceptance/denial of plaintiff’s evidentiary documents; defendant’s opinion on overall proceedings including plan to request evidence; and include evidence cited and explanatory documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory hearing agenda items
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparatory hearings typically discuss: dates and number of trials and matters for each; deadlines for submission of arguments and evidence (including comprehensive briefs and expert affidavits, number of submissions and length); whether to request time-consuming evidentiary methods (verification, appraisal, expert witness) and their deadlines; designation of technical advisor; holding technical explanatory sessions; whether to first hold claim construction hearing; handling pending correction petitions; parallel hearings for related cases; and confirmation/summary of disputed issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparatory hearings often conducted via conference call and supervised by a presiding (commissioned) judge; they set procedural schedule and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal technical explanatory session practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal technical explanatory session is held before hearing dates to increase the court’s understanding of technical issues; a technical examiner explains background technology and issues relating to the invention and prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike some civil patent cases where it may be omitted, internal technical explanatory sessions are held in almost all revocation suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing conduct in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings involve examination of documentary evidence and arguments of both parties, identification and sharing of key issues, oral argument on key issues, and applications for further evidence; revocation suits usually take more time than general civil suits and often close after the first round of intensive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revocation suits focus on technical issues (e.g., inventive step) rather than factual disputes; first hearing often arranged as technical explanatory session; arguments may be presented in foreign language with parties’ consent and court permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between revocation and civil patent suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Civil Procedure Act applies mutatis mutandis to revocation suits except as otherwise provided; revocation suits and civil patent suits have almost the same litigation and evidence collection procedures, though revocation suits typically contest fewer key issues and progress faster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds for invalidation may also be contended in infringement suits; the difference is scope and concurrency of issues (infringement suits cover scope of protection, invalidation, damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel handling of related cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Related cases with the same registration number are, in principle, allocated to the same judicial panel; if infringement and revocation cases for the same patent are pending concurrently before the same panel with same parties and need for parallel hearing is recognized, court will hold trials in parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must notify panels if related cases are allocated to different panels to enable reallocation procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence collection and ex officio examination
rubrics_metrics.description: In revocation suits the types of evidence and processes are similar to civil litigation; the court may examine evidence ex officio if necessary, but the principle of pleadings remains the governing rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex officio examination is supplementary and performed only to the extent of the evidence on record; Korea does not adopt a doctrine of court-conducted full fact-finding ex officio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal routes for revocation cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Court decisions in revocation cases may be appealed to the Supreme Court; appeal procedure follows the same rules as civil cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See civil appeal procedure (Section 8.8) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of court decision revoking IPTAB decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a court decision revoking an IPTAB decision becomes final and conclusive, the revoked decision becomes void and IPTAB must review the case and render another decision; the grounds on which revocation was rendered are binding upon the IPTAB with respect to the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example process provided showing steps from application to eventual examiner granting patent after judicial revocation is finalized and binding on IPTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of patent infringement (who infringes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who is neither a patentee nor an exclusive licensee and who practices a patented invention for business purposes without permission is committing infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee enjoys exclusive right for business purposes; exclusive and nonexclusive licensing regimes alter enforcement rights (see license-related criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and registration requirements for exclusive vs nonexclusive licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive license grants monopoly to licensee and must be registered to take effect; nonexclusive license does not grant monopoly, can be multiple, and registration is not needed to be effective between parties but is needed to be effective against third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive licensee may seek damages or injunction on their own; nonexclusive licensee generally may not seek damages or injunction. Common view: patentee may still seek injunction even when exclusive license granted over entire scope, but patentee cannot independently seek damages without joining the exclusive licensee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for established infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once infringement is established, patentee may seek: compensation for damages (or restitution of unjust enrichment), preliminary or permanent injunctions, disposal of means used to infringe, recovery of reputation; criminal liability may also apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory references: Article 750 Civil Act / Article 128(1) Patent Act for damages; Article 126 Patent Act for injunctions; Article 131 for reputation; Article 225 for criminal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required to establish infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee must prove ownership of the patent and that defendant has practiced the patent; defendant’s products or methods must fall within the scope of protection of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope of protection is determined by claim construction prior to infringement determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that scope of protection is determined by claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of protection is the objective scope determined by what is stated in the claims; claims must be construed before determining infringement, novelty, or inventive step and claim construction is a legal evaluation, not factual confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be construed objectively and reasonably based on claim wording, reference to detailed description/drawings, and general technical knowledge at filing; prosecution history may be referenced but should not be used to broaden or narrow claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal interpretation principle and reference to description/prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: Main reliance is on wording of the claims (literal interpretation), but descriptions/drawings and general technical knowledge should be given weight (reference to description); prosecution history (specs, amendments, written arguments, examiner opinions) may be consulted but not used to broaden or narrow claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptions/drawings to accurately understand technical meaning of claim language; avoid using prosecution history to alter claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement analysis by element-by-element comparison (all elements rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff breaks down disputed claim into elements and compares them to corresponding elements of defendant’s product/process; defendant may dispute element identification and courts ensure common understanding; infringement requires every element and their organic combination to be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-to-one comparison charts are often produced; if any element is missing, no infringement under literal all-elements rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Established when all claim elements and their organic combination, as specified by literal interpretation of the claims, are found in the defendant’s product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal matching of claim language and combination is required for literal infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by equivalence (requirements and burdens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement by equivalence is established when defendant’s elements are not literally identical but are equivalent, requiring positive and negative requirements: (i) identity of solution principles (same principle to solve problem); (ii) substantial identity of effects; (iii) easiness of replacement (person skilled would easily conceive replacement); (iv) not free-to-practice technology in public domain; (v) replaced element not purposely excluded from claim scope during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee bears burden for positive requirements; infringer bears burden for negative requirements. Determination requires identifying the essence of the technical idea underlying the patented solution in light of description and prior art; superficial feature deductions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement (constructive acts constituting infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing, assigning, leasing, importing, or offering to assign or lease a product exclusively used for manufacturing a patented product or practicing a patented process, when done for business purposes, are deemed infringement under Article 127(1) and (2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove indirect infringement, patentee must show use requirement (good is used in practicing invention), exclusivity requirement (alleged good is exclusively used for practicing invention), and business purpose; patentee has burden of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of responses: denials vs defenses and burden allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses are classed as denials (burden of proof on plaintiff) and defenses (burden of proof on defendant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the defendant denies infringement despite a prima facie showing, statutory obligations may require disclosure of actual product/process in use; failure may lead to presumption of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to disclose actual product/process when denying infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under amended Patent Act, defendant denying infringement after plaintiff's prima facie showing must disclose details of the product/process actually used; if defendant refuses without adequate justification, court may presume defendant committed the infringing act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shifts evidentiary advantage toward patentee where defendant withholds information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of rights defense and court review of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense that exercising patent rights is abusive when the patented invention lacks an inventive step; court is entitled to review and determine inventive step in infringement suit to decide this defense even before administrative invalidation is final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity requirement for 'lack of inventive step' is generally considered met in practice when judge finds lack of inventive step; also applicable to lack of novelty or sufficiency of description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-to-exploit technology defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may argue that their product/process only implements technology that was publicly known or easily derived from publicly known technology, making comparison to patent unnecessary to conclude non-infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense resembles inventive step analysis but compares defendant’s product to public knowledge; rarely used because defendants often prefer abuse-of-rights defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known technology defense (burden on defendant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may assert that patented invention consists only of technologies publicly known or in public use at filing; defendant bears burden to prove the invention is publicly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense may be asserted in addition to free-to-exploit but is less frequently used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent exhaustion (first sale doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reselling or using a patented product lawfully transferred from the patentee is generally acceptable and does not constitute infringement (patent right exhausted) for product inventions under Korean practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court acknowledges exhaustion when product is lawfully sold in Korea; exhaustion prevents patentee from extending patent effects to subsequent acts of assignee/buyer with regard to assigned product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited effect or lawful practice defenses (licenses and statutory/compulsory licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may assert that: the effect of the patent is limited (Articles 96, 181 Patent Act); they have an exclusive or nonexclusive license; they have a statutory license under specified Patent Act articles; or they are granted a compulsory license under specified articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are statutory grounds that, if proven, restrict patentee’s remedies or justify practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial case-management features and burden-relief provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent litigation faces evidence concentration with defendant possession of evidence; Patent Act shifts burdens and provides constructive presumptions and special provisions (e.g., Articles 129, 130, 127; Article 126-2 obligation to disclose actual product/process; Article 132 order to submit materials; Article 128-2 obligation to explain matters for appraisal) to protect patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory mechanisms aim to relieve patentees’ burden of proof; defendants may still assert justifying causes or statutory defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil patent procedure: filing, service, and trial scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil actions are initiated by filing complaint in court with jurisdiction over defendant’s residence or place of business; service is conducted by court; trials in Korea consist of multiple short trials spaced weeks apart, with first trial ordinarily scheduled two to three months after filing; patent trials are longer and may involve multiple hearings and technical presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical decision timelines: injunction-only main action ~8–12 months; cases with injunction and damages ~12–18 months. IP divisions and Patent Court provide practice directions for procedures at each level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic Case Filing System (ECFS) usage and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: ECFS enables paperless processing, electronic filing and management, uploading of court documents, notifications by email/SMS, and electronic access to case records by litigants and attorneys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ECFS is widely used though not mandatory; judges can retrieve files and display them in courtrooms; electronic files are closed to the public for privacy and security, but published decisions are publicly accessible online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial jurisdiction and exclusive forum for patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 24 Civil Procedure Act and Article 28-4 Court Organization Act, lawsuits concerning patent and listed IP rights fall under exclusive jurisdiction of the district court located where a high court is seated (with concurrent original jurisdiction to the Seoul Central District Court); Patent Court has exclusive jurisdiction over appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive jurisdiction under Article 24(2) invalidates agreements to the contrary; appeals of small claims patent cases go to the Patent Court regardless of usual appellate routing; exclusive jurisdiction does not apply to IP suits excluding patents/other listed IP rights, which follow ordinary jurisdictional rules.
